props.title: What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?

sections.content: What Ever Happened to Baby Jane (1962)? marks a pivotal moment in psychological horror, powered by the legendary offscreen rivalry between Bette Davis and Joan Crawford. Davis's unhinged portrayal of former child star Baby Jane Hudson terrorizing her wheelchair-bound sister Blanche (Crawford) created a whole subgenre: "psycho-biddy" or "hagsploitation" films. The film's claustrophobic atmosphere and grotesque makeup (Davis insisted on making herself look as hideous as possible) influenced later works like Misery (1990) and Sunset Boulevard (1950), exploring the dark side of fame and sibling rivalry.

sections.content: The film's impact on the horror-thriller genre can't be overstated. Director Robert Aldrich created a template for psychological torture that influenced films like Single White Female (1992) and The Hand That Rocks the Cradle (1992). The makeup transformation of Davis from aging former star to grotesque tormentor inspired countless horror films, including The Devil's Rejects (2005) and May (2002), where physical appearance reflects psychological deterioration.

The film's exploration of sisterly bonds turned toxic resonates through modern cinema. Sisters (1972) by Brian De Palma directly references the dynamic, while recent films like Black Swan (2010) and Hereditary (2018) echo its themes of family, jealousy, and psychological breakdown. The confined setting of the Hudson mansion became a blueprint for single-location thrillers. SUBHEAD: Impact on Female-Driven Horror

sections.content: What Ever Happened to Baby Jane? revolutionized how Hollywood portrayed aging actresses. Instead of fading away, Davis and Crawford created a new archetype of the "grande dame guignol" that influenced films like Death Becomes Her (1992) and The Others (2001). The film's success proved audiences would embrace older actresses in complex, villainous roles, paving the way for performers like Jessica Lange in American Horror Story (2011-present).
